title: "\"Significantly predicts\" when R² is 0.04: what open data reveal about a published regression"
subtitle: "Re-analysing an open data set with a Bayesian beta-binomial model in brms, and asking what a small slope can and cannot say"

```{r}
#| label: LoadPack
#| include: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(brms)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(readxl)

Plot_theme <- theme_classic() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 15, hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    axis.line = element_line(colour = "black", linewidth = 1),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "black", size = 13),
    axis.text = element_text(colour = "black", size = 11),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    legend.title = element_text(colour = "black", face = "bold", size = 12),
    legend.text = element_text(colour = "black", size = 10)
  )

dir.create("plots", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Medium has no tables, so every table is also saved as an image
save_table <- function(df, file) {
  gt::gt(df) |>
    gt::tab_options(table.font.size = 14, data_row.padding = gt::px(6)) |>
    gt::gtsave(file.path("plots", file), zoom = 5, expand = 10)
}

# One colour per concept, used in every figure
cols <- c(lm = "#D55E00", bayes = "#0072B2", adj = "#009E73")
dx_cols <- c(HC = "#009E73", SCC = "#56B4E9", MCI = "#E69F00", AD = "#D55E00", bvFTD = "#CC79A7")
```

Open a paper in any biomedical field and search for "predicted". A recent study of social cognition in ageing [@fittipaldi2024] says that "advanced age significantly predicted worse emotion recognition", and describes the analysis as a way to "evaluate the predictive value of age". The figure behind it shows 998 people, a red line sloping gently down through a cloud of grey dots, and an R² of 0.04.

I have told authors, as reviewer 2, that the problem was not their extreme observations but the statistical model they had chosen. Here the problem is a word. "Predicted" does the work of "was associated with", and the reader is left to guess how much prediction 4% of the variance buys. I ask that question with the authors' own open data. My claim is narrow: a slope with R² = 0.04 describes a small association, offers almost no evidence of prediction, and cannot tell you what the association is made of. Here, a good part of it is made of who is old.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you'll take away

- How to check that a published number reproduces from open data, and what to do when a data transformation is not documented.
- Why the same slope and R² fit very different pictures, and which graphs and models tell them apart.
- How to use a beta-binomial model in `brms` to produce what a clinician can judge: expected scores by decade, the probability that a younger person scores higher, and what changes when you account for diagnosis.
:::

One sentence is not the paper. The headline models in that study are support vector regressions, and the authors report that age did not emerge as a contributor and that the effects of age and diagnosis "attenuate or vanish" once other factors are considered. I agree with where the paper lands, and I do not object to prediction as a goal. My objection is to the first analysis, the one that opens with "predicted", because I see that pattern everywhere. I model only emotion recognition; the other two outcomes need other likelihoods (mentalizing is 40 points from ten stories, not 40 independent trials). I use `brms` [@brms-2] and the `tidyverse`.

# What the paper prints, and what the open data reproduce

I started this post believing the raw data were not shared, and began to reverse-engineer the figure from the printed numbers. Then I read the data availability statement: the anonymised data and code are on [GitHub](https://github.com/AI-BrainLat-team/Global-Mini-SEA) and the Open Science Framework. I am glad I looked, and the authors deserve credit. The repository has no licence file, so the chunk below downloads `Data/Base.xlsx` at render time instead of copying it into this folder.

```{r}
#| label: LoadData

n_trials <- 35
src   <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AI-BrainLat-team/Global-Mini-SEA/main/Data/Base.xlsx"
local <- "data/Base.xlsx"
if (!file.exists(local)) download.file(src, local, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
raw <- read_excel(local)

mini <- raw |>
  transmute(
    # diagnosis codes decoded by matching group sizes to the figure caption
    dx = factor(diagnosis_specify, levels = c(1, 4, 5, 2, 3), labels = c("HC", "SCC", "MCI", "AD", "bvFTD")),
    income = factor(country_class), sex = factor(gender),
    age = Edad_procesada, educ = years_education,
    fer = mini_sea_fer, tom = mini_sea_tom, total = mini_sea_total
  ) |>
  mutate(age_dec = (age - 72) / 10,                 # age in decades, centred at 72
         educ5 = (educ - 12) / 5,                   # education in 5-year units, centred at 12
         k = round(fer * n_trials / 15))            # photos identified correctly, out of 35

table(mini$dx)
```

The five diagnostic groups are healthy controls (HC), subjective cognitive complaints (SCC), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), Alzheimer's disease (AD) and behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD). The file has 998 rows, no missing values in these columns, and group sizes that match the figure caption. The paper prints a table of simple regressions of each score on age (Extended Data Table 1). Do the open data return it?

```{r}
#| label: Reproduce

reg <- function(y) {
  m <- lm(y ~ mini$age); s <- summary(m)
  c(slope = unname(coef(m)[2]), R2 = s$r.squared, F = unname(s$fstatistic[1]),
    P = unname(pf(s$fstatistic[1], 1, s$fstatistic[3], lower.tail = FALSE)))
}
real <- t(sapply(list(mini$fer, mini$tom, mini$total), reg))

repro_tab <- (
  data.frame(
    Outcome = c("Emotion recognition", "Mentalizing", "Total"),
    `Printed: slope, F, P` = sprintf("%.2f, %.2f, %.3g", c(-0.05, -0.05, -0.1), c(47.49, 22.22, 42), c(9.792e-12, 2.78e-06, 1.435e-10)),
    `Open data: slope, R², F, P` = sprintf("%.3f, %.3f, %.2f, %.3g", real[, "slope"], real[, "R2"], real[, "F"], real[, "P"]),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
)
save_table(repro_tab, "01_Table_Reproduction.png")
knitr::kable(repro_tab)
```

Yes. Emotion recognition returns F = `r sprintf("%.2f", real[1, "F"])` and P = `r sprintf("%.3g", real[1, "P"])`, the printed 47.49 and 9.792e-12; the slope is `r sprintf("%.3f", real[1, "slope"])` (the paper rounds to −0.05) and R² is `r sprintf("%.3f", real[1, "R2"])`. Mentalizing and the total score match too. That is what reproducibility looks like, and I do not take it for granted.

## What is still missing

The Methods say each score was "converted to a score of 15", not how. With 35 photos, the natural reading is correct answers times 15/35. Check it:

```{r}
#| label: Lattice

grid_dist    <- abs(mini$fer - 15 * mini$k / n_trials)
share_on_grid <- mean(grid_dist < 0.0101)      # two-decimal rounding or truncation of 15 * k / 35
off_grid     <- mini$fer[grid_dist >= 0.0101]
c(share_on_grid = share_on_grid, n_off_grid = length(off_grid), max_error = max(grid_dist))
head(sort(table(off_grid), decreasing = TRUE), 5)
slope_all  <- coef(lm(fer ~ age, mini))[2]
slope_grid <- coef(lm(fer ~ age, mini[grid_dist < 0.0101, ]))[2]
```

For `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * share_on_grid)`% of participants the score sits exactly on that grid. For the other `r length(off_grid)` it does not, and I do not know why: a different test version, harmonisation across countries or imputation are all possible. I found no code for Figure 1 or for the conversion in the repository, though I have not opened every notebook. For the model I round every score to the nearest of the 36 possible values, a shift of at most `r sprintf("%.2f", max(grid_dist))` points; using only the on-grid participants gives a pooled slope of `r sprintf("%.3f", slope_grid)` instead of `r sprintf("%.3f", slope_all)` points per year.

This is small, and it is why I care about open science as more than a slogan. Shared data without the code that transformed it lets you reproduce a number but not interpret it. I had to guess how the scores were built, and my guess was right for four participants in five; a reader with less time would never notice the fifth. The conversion script costs the authors almost nothing, because they already wrote it, and it saves everyone else from assumptions about someone else's data. In the lab we write the dilutions and exposure times next to the blot. This is the same duty.

# Same numbers, eight different pictures

A slope and an R² are two numbers; a scatter plot has a thousand. I built seven stories about what ageing does to this score, each a beta-binomial process on the 35-photo test using the 998 real ages, each calibrated to the printed slope and R². The eighth panel is the real data.

```{r}
#| label: PanelWorlds
#| code-fold: true

dec      <- function(a) (a - 72) / 10
bb_score <- function(mu, phi)
  15 * rbinom(length(mu), n_trials, rbeta(length(mu), mu * phi, (1 - mu) * phi)) / n_trials

panel_gen <- list(
  "Steady decline in everyone" = function(a)
    bb_score(plogis(0.9401 - 0.1787 * dec(a)), 13),
  "Decline only after 75" = function(a)
    bb_score(plogis(1.06 - 0.5888 * pmax(a - 75, 0) / 10), 13),
  "Decline only before 70" = function(a)
    bb_score(plogis(1.666 - 0.4093 * pmin(pmax(a - 50, 0), 20) / 10), 13),
  "Variance grows with age" = function(a)
    bb_score(plogis(0.9461 - 0.1864 * dec(a)), exp(log(13) - 0.6 * dec(a))),
  "A growing minority is impaired" = function(a) {
    imp <- rbinom(length(a), 1, plogis(-1.533 + 1.089 * dec(a)))
    bb_score(ifelse(imp == 1, 0.52, 0.76), ifelse(imp == 1, 14, 40)) },
  "A few extreme low scorers, all old" = function(a) {
    imp <- rbinom(length(a), 1, plogis(-4.324 + 2.534 * dec(a)))
    bb_score(ifelse(imp == 1, 0.28, 0.74), ifelse(imp == 1, 18, 40)) },
  "Half decline fast, half not at all" = function(a) {
    g <- rbinom(length(a), 1, 0.5)
    bb_score(plogis(0.9473 - 2 * g * 0.1791 * dec(a)), 13) }
)

# keep the seed whose sample lands closest to the real slope and R2
pick_world <- function(gen, label) {
  fits <- sapply(1:400, function(s) {
    set.seed(s); y <- gen(mini$age); m <- lm(y ~ mini$age); c(coef(m)[2], summary(m)$r.squared)
  })
  s <- which.min(((fits[1, ] - real[1, "slope"]) / 0.002)^2 + ((fits[2, ] - real[1, "R2"]) / 0.004)^2)
  set.seed(s); data.frame(age = mini$age, y = gen(mini$age), scenario = label)
}

scenario_order <- c(names(panel_gen), "The real data")
panel_df <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(panel_gen), function(nm) pick_world(panel_gen[[nm]], nm)),
  data.frame(age = mini$age, y = mini$fer, scenario = "The real data")
)

panel_stats <- panel_df |>
  group_by(scenario) |>
  summarise(slope = coef(lm(y ~ age))[2], r2 = summary(lm(y ~ age))$r.squared,
            mean = mean(y), sd = sd(y), .groups = "drop")

panel_df <- panel_df |>
  left_join(panel_stats, by = "scenario") |>
  mutate(lab = sprintf("%d. %s\nslope %.3f, R² %.3f", match(scenario, scenario_order), scenario, slope, r2),
         lab = factor(lab, levels = unique(lab[order(match(scenario, scenario_order))])))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-panel
#| fig-cap: "Eight clouds with almost the same slope and R² (n = 998 each, the same 998 ages). Panels 1 to 7 are simulated; panel 8 is the real data. Grey points are people (jittered); the red line is the OLS fit the paper shows; the blue curve is a smoother that follows the data."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6.5

p_panel <- ggplot(panel_df, aes(age, y)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.3, height = 0.2, alpha = 0.3, size = 1, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = cols["lm"], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.9, se = FALSE, colour = cols["bayes"], linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~lab, ncol = 4) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 15), breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 15)) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Emotion recognition (0-15)") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 9))
ggsave("plots/02_Fig_Panel_Eight_Clouds.png", p_panel, width = 11, height = 6.5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
p_panel
```

The red lines are the same line, and it is all the paper's panel shows. The blue smoother separates some pictures: a collapse after 80 (panels 2 and 6) and a drop that then stops (panel 3). It cannot separate 1, 4, 5 and 7: everybody declines a little, the cloud fans out, a growing minority is impaired, or some people decline fast and the rest not at all. Those four tell very different stories and look alike. The real data decline until about 80 and then flatten, nearer panels 3 and 4 than 2 or 6, and a scatter plot cannot say more. The seven are constructions: they show that two numbers cannot tell stories apart, not which one the data follow. To find out what the slope is made of, we need other variables.

# Who is old in this sample?

The paper's Figure 1c shows that diagnosis moves scores by several points, but the age panel adjusts for nothing. How do age and diagnosis relate?

```{r}
#| label: GroupTable

grp_tab <- mini |>
  group_by(Group = dx) |>
  summarise(n = n(), `Mean age` = mean(age), `SD age` = sd(age), `Mean score (0-15)` = mean(fer),
            `Income class 1 (%)` = 100 * mean(income == "1"), .groups = "drop")
save_table(dplyr::mutate(grp_tab, dplyr::across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 1))), "03_Table_Groups.png")
knitr::kable(grp_tab, digits = 1)
eta_age_dx <- summary(lm(age ~ dx, mini))$r.squared
```

The groups are not the same age. SCC participants average `r sprintf("%.0f", grp_tab$"Mean age"[2])` years and MCI participants `r sprintf("%.0f", grp_tab$"Mean age"[3])`, against `r sprintf("%.0f", grp_tab$"Mean age"[1])` for healthy controls, and the groups with the lowest scores are among the oldest. Diagnosis alone accounts for `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * eta_age_dx)`% of the variance in age. Every SCC and MCI participant comes from income class 1, which echoes a limitation the authors acknowledge: these two groups were enrolled in a single country and centre. Age, diagnosis and place are tangled.

```{r}
#| label: fig-groups
#| fig-cap: "Emotion recognition by age and diagnostic group (real data). Coloured lines are within-group OLS fits; the black dashed line is the pooled fit the paper shows."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.8

p_groups <- ggplot(mini, aes(age, fer, colour = dx)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.3, height = 0.2, alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = dx_cols) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Emotion recognition (0-15)", colour = NULL) +
  Plot_theme
ggsave("plots/04_Fig_Groups_By_Age.png", p_groups, width = 7.5, height = 4.8, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
p_groups
```

Most coloured lines are flatter than the dashed one, and the groups sit at different heights. The pooled slope blends "older people score lower" with "the groups that score lower are older".

# A model that knows the scale

Pause and predict. Take one person aged 55 and one aged 85 from this sample. How often does the younger one score higher? Write a number down; we will compute it.

The scores are counts out of 35 photos with a wall at the top, which a Gaussian regression ignores (its prediction band for a 55-year-old runs above the maximum possible score). A beta-binomial regression in `brms` respects it: the number correct is binomial, with a success probability that is itself Beta-distributed, so people may vary more than item noise allows. We start with the paper's analysis, age alone.

```{r}
#| label: FitPooled
#| results: hide

priors <- c(
  prior(normal(1, 1.5), class = Intercept),   # logit of ~0.75, with room to move
  prior(normal(0, 1),   class = b),           # per decade / per unit, on the logit scale
  prior(gamma(2, 0.1),  class = phi)          # between-person variability
)

fit_pool <- brm(
  k | trials(35) ~ age_dec,
  data = mini, family = beta_binomial(), prior = priors,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123,
  file = "models/Fit_pool"
)
```

The priors are weakly informative: they exclude absurd effects but push the data nowhere. Can the model generate data that look like ours?

```{r}
#| label: fig-ppc
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check for the pooled beta-binomial model. Bars show the observed number of participants at each raw score; points and lines show 100 simulated data sets."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4

p_ppc <- pp_check(fit_pool, type = "bars", ndraws = 100) +
  labs(x = "Photos identified correctly (of 35)", y = "Participants") +
  Plot_theme
ggsave("plots/05_Fig_Posterior_Predictive_Check.png", p_ppc, width = 7, height = 4, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
p_ppc
```

It reproduces the skewed shape and the ceiling. It is still a simplification: photos differ in difficulty, and a blind guess among seven emotions is right one time in seven. An item-response model would be closer.

A logit coefficient is not what anyone wants to know. I want points lost per decade on the paper's 0 to 15 scale: predict everyone's score at their observed age and again ten years later, multiply by 15/35, and average the difference over posterior draws so the answer carries its uncertainty.

```{r}
#| label: DecadeEffect

decade_effect <- function(fit, data) {
  up <- transform(data, age_dec = age_dec + 1)
  15 / n_trials * rowMeans(posterior_epred(fit, newdata = up) - posterior_epred(fit, newdata = data))
}

summarise_draws_simple <- function(x) {
  c(mean = mean(x), lwr = unname(quantile(x, 0.025)), upr = unname(quantile(x, 0.975)))
}

eff_pool <- decade_effect(fit_pool, mini)
round(summarise_draws_simple(eff_pool), 2)
```

Per decade the expected score drops by `r sprintf("%.2f", -mean(eff_pool))` points (95% credible interval `r sprintf("%.2f", -quantile(eff_pool, 0.975))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", -quantile(eff_pool, 0.025))` points lost), about a quarter of the between-person standard deviation (`r sprintf("%.1f", sd(mini$fer))`). That is a real shift, clearly not zero, and modest. The better model changes the slope little; it stops us from saying wrong things around it.

# What is the slope made of?

Now give the model what the pooled regression ignores: diagnosis, then diagnosis plus income class, sex and education. I also fit healthy controls alone, where no disease confounds age.

```{r}
#| label: FitAdjusted
#| results: hide

fit_dx <- brm(
  k | trials(35) ~ age_dec + dx,
  data = mini, family = beta_binomial(), prior = priors,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123,
  file = "models/Fit_dx"
)

fit_full <- brm(
  k | trials(35) ~ age_dec + dx + income + sex + educ5,
  data = mini, family = beta_binomial(), prior = priors,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123,
  file = "models/Fit_full"
)

mini_hc <- filter(mini, dx == "HC")
fit_hc <- update(fit_pool, newdata = mini_hc, seed = 123, file = "models/Fit_hc")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest
#| fig-cap: "Change in expected emotion recognition per decade of age, under four beta-binomial models (real data). Points are posterior means; bars are 95% credible intervals."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.8

eff <- list(
  "Age only\n(the paper's analysis)" = eff_pool,
  "+ diagnosis" = decade_effect(fit_dx, mini),
  "+ diagnosis, income,\nsex, education" = decade_effect(fit_full, mini),
  "Healthy controls only\n(age only, n = 316)" = decade_effect(fit_hc, mini_hc)
)

eff_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(eff), function(nm) {
  s <- summarise_draws_simple(eff[[nm]])
  data.frame(model = nm, mean = s["mean"], lwr = s["lwr"], upr = s["upr"])
})) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = rev(names(eff))),
         type = ifelse(grepl("Age only\n", model, fixed = TRUE), "pooled", "adjusted"))

p_forest <- ggplot(eff_df, aes(mean, model, colour = type)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lwr, xmax = upr), linewidth = 1, size = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pooled = unname(cols["bayes"]), adjusted = unname(cols["adj"]))) +
  labs(x = "Change in expected score per decade (points)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  Plot_theme
ggsave("plots/06_Fig_Forest_Decade_Effect.png", p_forest, width = 7.5, height = 3.8, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
p_forest
```

The paper's analysis gives `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(eff[[1]]))` points per decade. Once diagnosis is in the model the estimate falls to `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(eff[[2]]))` (95% credible interval `r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(eff[[2]], 0.025))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(eff[[2]], 0.975))`), and with income class, sex and education to `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(eff[[3]]))` (`r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(eff[[3]], 0.025))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(eff[[3]], 0.975))`). Among healthy controls it is `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(eff[[4]]))` (`r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(eff[[4]], 0.025))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(eff[[4]], 0.975))`), so ageing within a group is not zero either. The pooled slope was not wrong; it was an average over a mixture, and the mixture, not ageing within a group, accounts for much of it.

Three cautions keep me from overselling this. First, diagnosis can be downstream of ageing: if part of what makes someone 78 and MCI is ageing, adjusting for diagnosis removes a share of the true age effect together with the confounding. Second, the design is cross-sectional. These are differences between older and younger people, born in different years and with different schooling, not a decline measured within one person, so `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(eff[[3]]))` is not "the pure effect of ageing" either. Third, the study spans nine countries and 13 sites, and the file holds only a two-level income class; with the full data I would add a varying intercept such as `(1 | country)`. The adjusted number is a more defensible description than the pooled one, and the sentence "age significantly predicted" is silent about which of these quantities it is.

# Making the result legible: a table and two curves

A coefficient is a poor way to tell a person what to expect. I want the expected score at each age, how much individuals vary around it, and how many fall below a cutoff someone might care about. For each posterior draw I set everyone's age to the value of interest, keep their diagnosis, sex, income class and education as observed, and average the score distribution over the 998 people.

```{r}
#| label: PmfFunctions

# Score distribution (36 possible photo counts) at a given age, averaged over the people in `data`
pmf_std <- function(fit, data, at_age, ids = round(seq(1, ndraws(fit), length.out = 400))) {
  phi <- as_draws_df(fit)$phi[ids]
  nd  <- transform(data, age_dec = (at_age - 72) / 10)    # `at_age`: `age` would be masked by the column in `data`
  mu  <- posterior_epred(fit, newdata = nd, draw_ids = ids) / n_trials     # draws x people
  sapply(0:n_trials, function(k)
    rowMeans(exp(lchoose(n_trials, k) + lbeta(k + mu * phi, n_trials - k + (1 - mu) * phi) -
                   lbeta(mu * phi, (1 - mu) * phi))))
}

score_grid <- 15 * (0:n_trials) / n_trials
ages_eval  <- seq(55, 85, by = 5)
pm_pool <- lapply(ages_eval, function(a) pmf_std(fit_pool, mini, a))
pm_full <- lapply(ages_eval, function(a) pmf_std(fit_full, mini, a))
names(pm_pool) <- names(pm_full) <- ages_eval

# probability that a person from P1 scores higher than one from P2 (ties count as half)
p_higher <- function(P1, P2) {
  cdf1 <- t(apply(P1, 1, cumsum))
  rowSums(P2 * (1 - cdf1)) + 0.5 * rowSums(P1 * P2)
}

q <- function(x, p) unname(quantile(x, p))
```

```{r}
#| label: ExpectedTable

ages_tab <- c(55, 65, 75, 85)
cell <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f (%.1f to %.1f)", mean(x), q(x, 0.025), q(x, 0.975))
share <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%% (%.0f to %.0f)", 100 * mean(x), 100 * q(x, 0.025), 100 * q(x, 0.975))
range90 <- function(P) {
  cdf <- cumsum(colMeans(P))
  sprintf("%.1f and %.1f", score_grid[which(cdf >= 0.05)[1]], score_grid[which(cdf >= 0.95)[1]])
}

exp_tab <- bind_rows(lapply(ages_tab, function(a) {
  Pp <- pm_pool[[as.character(a)]]; Pf <- pm_full[[as.character(a)]]
  data.frame(
    Age = a,
    `Expected score, age only` = cell(Pp %*% score_grid),
    `Expected score, adjusted` = cell(Pf %*% score_grid),
    `90% of individuals between (adjusted)` = range90(Pf),
    `Share scoring 9 or less, age only` = share(rowSums(Pp[, 1:22])),
    `Share scoring 9 or less, adjusted` = share(rowSums(Pf[, 1:22])),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))
save_table(exp_tab, "07_Table_Expected_Scores.png")
knitr::kable(exp_tab, align = "cccccc")
```

Read it by columns. The intervals for the average are narrow; the range that holds 90% of individuals is about six points wide, and the ranges at 55 and 85 overlap almost entirely. Both are true at once, and the paper's figure shows only the first.

The last two columns are where I would look as a clinician. The cutoff of 9 out of 15 is mine and arbitrary; use your clinic's. From 55 to 85 the share at or below it goes from `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(rowSums(pm_pool[["55"]][, 1:22])))`% to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(rowSums(pm_pool[["85"]][, 1:22])))`% in the pooled model and from `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(rowSums(pm_full[["55"]][, 1:22])))`% to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(rowSums(pm_full[["85"]][, 1:22])))`% once we adjust. The adjusted figure at 55 is higher because it keeps the diagnostic mix of the whole sample at every age, patients included, while the pooled line treats a 55-year-old as healthy as the youngest people recruited. Only `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(mini$age > 90))`% of the sample is older than 90, so the table stops at 85.

Two more views:

```{r}
#| label: fig-gap-threshold
#| fig-cap: "Left: probability that a 55-year-old scores higher than someone older by the age gap shown (ties count as half); bands are 95% credible intervals. Right: posterior probability that the true loss per decade exceeds a given number of points; the dashed line marks one photo (15/35 points)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

gaps <- seq(5, 30, by = 5)
gap_df <- bind_rows(lapply(c("Age only", "Adjusted"), function(m) {
  pm <- if (m == "Age only") pm_pool else pm_full
  ps <- sapply(gaps, function(g) p_higher(pm[["55"]], pm[[as.character(55 + g)]]))
  data.frame(model = m, gap = gaps, mean = colMeans(ps),
             lo = apply(ps, 2, q, 0.025), hi = apply(ps, 2, q, 0.975))
}))

loss_pool <- -eff_pool
loss_full <- -eff[[3]]
thr_df <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(model = "Age only", thr = seq(0, 1.2, by = 0.01)),
  data.frame(model = "Adjusted", thr = seq(0, 1.2, by = 0.01))
) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(p = mean((if (model == "Age only") loss_pool else loss_full) > thr)) |>
  ungroup()
one_photo <- 15 / n_trials
model_cols <- c("Age only" = unname(cols["bayes"]), "Adjusted" = unname(cols["adj"]))

p_gap <- ggplot(gap_df, aes(gap, mean, colour = model, fill = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_cols) + scale_fill_manual(values = model_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.45, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Age gap (years)", y = "Probability the younger scores higher", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  Plot_theme

p_thr <- ggplot(thr_df, aes(thr, p, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = one_photo, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Loss per decade (points, 0-15 scale)", y = "Posterior probability loss is larger", colour = NULL) +
  Plot_theme

p_both <- p_gap + p_thr
ggsave("plots/08_Fig_Gap_And_Threshold.png", p_both, width = 10, height = 4, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
p_both
```

```{r}
#| label: GapNumbers
g10_pool <- gap_df$mean[gap_df$model == "Age only" & gap_df$gap == 10]
g30_pool <- gap_df$mean[gap_df$model == "Age only" & gap_df$gap == 30]
g30_full <- gap_df$mean[gap_df$model == "Adjusted" & gap_df$gap == 30]
```

The left panel is the one I would put in an abstract. Pooled, a 10-year gap lands on the younger person's side `r round(100 * g10_pool)`% of the time and a 30-year gap `r round(100 * g30_pool)`%, which answers the question I posed earlier; adjusted, the 30-year figure is `r round(100 * g30_full)`%. The right panel replaces "the interval excludes zero" with a question you can answer yourself: how large would a loss have to be to matter to you, and how probable is that?

## Does this reduction matter clinically?

I cannot answer that from these data, because relevance needs an anchor outside the model. Three candidates:

- The test itself. One photo is 15/35 = `r sprintf("%.2f", one_photo)` points. The pooled estimate is a loss of about `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(loss_pool) * n_trials / 15)` photos per decade, and the adjusted one about `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(loss_full) * n_trials / 15)`. The probability that the loss exceeds one photo per decade is `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(loss_pool > one_photo))`% in the first case and `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(loss_full > one_photo))`% in the second.
- A known contrast. Healthy controls score on average `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(mini$fer[mini$dx == "HC"]) - mean(mini$fer[mini$dx == "MCI"]))` points above people with mild cognitive impairment. The pooled loss per decade is about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(loss_pool) / (mean(mini$fer[mini$dx == "HC"]) - mean(mini$fer[mini$dx == "MCI"])))`% of that gap; the adjusted one about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(loss_full) / (mean(mini$fer[mini$dx == "HC"]) - mean(mini$fer[mini$dx == "MCI"])))`%.
- Something that matters to a person. Does a lower score here go together with worse daily functioning, a missed diagnosis or a change in treatment? Nothing in this data set can say.

So it stays a question for the researcher, not the model. How much does one person's score vary between two sessions when nothing in their life has changed? If that exceeds the loss across thirty years, individual change is invisible to the test. And is a small loss shared by everyone a different thing from a larger loss concentrated in a minority (panels 5 and 6 above)? The table and curves do not decide; they let you ask with numbers instead of stars.

# Does age improve out-of-sample prediction?

Does age improve predictions for people the model has not seen? Leave-one-out cross-validation [@vehtari2016] estimates exactly that. I compare six models, with and without age and the other variables.

```{r}
#| label: LooCompare
#| results: hide

fit_null <- brm(
  k | trials(35) ~ 1,
  data = mini, family = beta_binomial(),
  prior = c(prior(normal(1, 1.5), class = Intercept), prior(gamma(2, 0.1), class = phi)),
  chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 123,
  file = "models/Fit_null"
)
fit_dx_only <- update(fit_dx, formula. = k | trials(35) ~ dx, seed = 123, file = "models/Fit_dx_only")
fit_cov <- update(fit_full, formula. = k | trials(35) ~ dx + income + sex + educ5, seed = 123, file = "models/Fit_cov")

# Pointwise log-likelihood of the beta-binomial, written out so that `loo` can use it
loo_bb <- function(fit, data) {
  phi <- as_draws_df(fit)$phi
  mu  <- posterior_epred(fit, newdata = data) / n_trials          # draws x participants
  k   <- matrix(data$k, nrow(mu), ncol(mu), byrow = TRUE)
  ll  <- lchoose(n_trials, k) + lbeta(k + mu * phi, n_trials - k + (1 - mu) * phi) -
    lbeta(mu * phi, (1 - mu) * phi)
  loo::loo(ll)
}

loo_all <- loo_compare(list(
  `intercept only` = loo_bb(fit_null, mini),
  `age` = loo_bb(fit_pool, mini),
  `diagnosis` = loo_bb(fit_dx_only, mini),
  `age + diagnosis` = loo_bb(fit_dx, mini),
  `diagnosis + income, sex, education` = loo_bb(fit_cov, mini),
  `age + diagnosis + income, sex, education` = loo_bb(fit_full, mini)
))
```

```{r}
#| label: LooTable
loo_tab <- data.frame(Model = rownames(loo_all), round(loo_all[, c("elpd_diff", "se_diff")], 1), row.names = NULL)
save_table(loo_tab, "09_Table_LOO.png")
knitr::kable(round(loo_all[, c("elpd_diff", "se_diff")], 1))
gain_age <- loo_all["age + diagnosis + income, sex, education", "elpd_diff"] -
  loo_all["diagnosis + income, sex, education", "elpd_diff"]
```

The best model sits at zero; the others are differences in expected log predictive density. Age alone improves on the intercept-only model but trails any model that knows the diagnosis. The comparison that matters is the last pair: adding age to diagnosis, income class, sex and education changes the score by `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(gain_age))` units, against a standard error of `r sprintf("%.1f", loo_all["diagnosis + income, sex, education", "se_diff"])`, or `r sprintf("%.3f", abs(gain_age) / nrow(mini))` per person. Age alone beats the intercept-only model by a wide margin, and that is the whole content of "significantly predicts". It is a statement about a pooled association, not about a variable that helps predict anyone once the diagnosis is known.

# Your turn

- Would you accept "age was associated with a lower score of about half a point per decade (95% CrI …)" in a results section, or is the probability that a younger person scores higher the better single number? I lean towards reporting both, plus the adjusted version, but I can be argued out of it.
- Which "predicted" sentence in your own field would survive this treatment? Is there an open data set behind it that you could check?
- Where does your own pipeline convert, harmonise or impute values before they reach the analysis, and is that step written down anywhere a stranger could find it?

I read and answer every comment, including the ones that say I am being unfair to a descriptive analysis.
